hints: Look at what each symbol measures: $\text{A}$ for current, $\text{kg}$ for mass, $\text{C}$ for charge and $\text{s}$ for time.
Recall the seven SI base units include the ampere, kilogram and second, but electric charge is not a base quantity.
Check which quantity can be written as a product of other units, using $Q = It$ with charge in $\text{A s}$.
walkthrough: Identify the quantities: $\text{A}$ is current, $\text{kg}$ is mass, $\text{C}$ is electric charge and $\text{s}$ is time.
State the rule: SI base units cannot be expressed in terms of other units, while derived units can.
Recall three of these are base units: ampere for current, kilogram for mass, and second for time.
Show the derived unit: charge follows $Q = It$, so $1 \text{ C} = 1 \text{ A s}$.
Therefore the coulomb is built from base units and is not itself a base unit. This is option C.

options.A: The ampere, $\text{A}$, is the SI base unit for electric current.
options.B: The kilogram, $\text{kg}$, is the SI base unit for mass.
options.C: The coulomb, $\text{C}$, is a derived unit for charge, defined as $\text{A s}$, not a base unit.
options.D: The second, $\text{s}$, is the SI base unit for time.
